purpose: The standard way to ask someone about their job when you have just met.

conversation.speaker: A
conversation.text: Hi, I'm Alex. What do you do?

conversation.speaker: B
conversation.text: I'm a nurse — I work at the hospital on Green Street. How about you?

conversation.speaker: A
conversation.text: I'm in software. Mostly boring meetings, if I'm honest.

keyExpressions: How long have you been doing that?
remember: In almost every social context this is asking about work, not hobbies.
Always return the question. Answering and stopping ends the conversation immediately.

purpose: The default Monday morning opener with colleagues.

conversation.speaker: A
conversation.text: Morning — how was your weekend?

conversation.speaker: B
conversation.text: Really good, thanks. We went to my sister's for lunch. Yours?

conversation.speaker: A
conversation.text: Quiet one. I finally finished that series everyone's talking about.

remember: A one-line answer plus a return question is the expected shape. Nobody wants a full account.

purpose: A simple way to learn about someone's background early in a conversation.

conversation.speaker: A
conversation.text: Where are you from originally?

conversation.speaker: B
conversation.text: Kerala, in the south of India. I moved here six years ago.

conversation.speaker: A
conversation.text: Six years — do you get back often?

conversation.speaker: B
conversation.text: Once a year, usually in December.

keyExpressions: How long have you been here?
remember: Adding 'originally' makes it clear you mean where they grew up, not where they live now.
Follow the answer with a real question. 'Oh, nice' closes the topic instead of opening it.

purpose: Find a shared connection at a party, wedding, or event.

conversation.speaker: A
conversation.text: So how do you know Priya?

conversation.speaker: B
conversation.text: We were at university together. You?

conversation.speaker: A
conversation.text: We work together — I've heard a lot about those university years.

conversation.speaker: B
conversation.text: Whatever she told you, it's exaggerated.

keyExpressions: I've heard a lot about you.
remember: This is the standard opener at any event with a shared host. It gives you an immediate topic.

purpose: Start a conversation with someone at a venue or event you are both attending.

conversation.speaker: A
conversation.text: Have you been to one of these before?

conversation.speaker: B
conversation.text: First time. Is it always this busy?

conversation.speaker: A
conversation.text: Usually, yes. The talks in the afternoon are the good part.

conversation.speaker: B
conversation.text: Good to know. Which one are you going to?

keyExpressions: Which one are you going to?
remember: Asking about the shared situation is the easiest opener — you already know you have it in common.

purpose: Ask why someone is at an event, in a slightly more interesting way than 'why are you here'.

conversation.speaker: A
conversation.text: So what brings you to the conference?

conversation.speaker: B
conversation.text: We're launching something similar next year, so I'm here to steal ideas.

conversation.speaker: A
conversation.text: Honest, at least. Found any yet?

conversation.speaker: B
conversation.text: Two, and it's only lunchtime.

remember: 'Why are you here?' can sound suspicious. 'What brings you here?' asks the same thing warmly.

purpose: The Friday counterpart to 'how was your weekend'.

conversation.speaker: A
conversation.text: Any plans for the weekend?

conversation.speaker: B
conversation.text: Nothing much — might go to the market on Saturday. You?

conversation.speaker: A
conversation.text: My brother's visiting, so probably a lot of cooking.

remember: 'Nothing much' is a perfectly good answer. English small talk does not require impressive plans.

term: How long have you worked here?
purpose: Open a conversation with a new colleague and find common ground.

conversation.speaker: A
conversation.text: How long have you worked here?

conversation.speaker: B
conversation.text: Just over two years. You're new, aren't you?

conversation.speaker: A
conversation.text: Third week. Still learning where everything is.

conversation.speaker: B
conversation.text: The coffee machine on this floor is broken, so that's your first lesson.

keyExpressions: How long have you worked here?
remember: The present perfect is required here because the person still works there: 'have you worked', not 'did you work'.

purpose: The safest possible opener with a stranger, especially in Britain.

conversation.speaker: A
conversation.text: Miserable out there, isn't it?

conversation.speaker: B
conversation.text: Awful. And they said it would clear up by noon.

conversation.speaker: A
conversation.text: They always say that.

keyExpressions: They said it would clear up.
Is it supposed to rain later?
remember: The tag question ('isn't it?') is what makes it an invitation to talk rather than a statement.
Nobody genuinely cares about the weather here — it is a signal that you are open to conversation.

purpose: Start a work conversation that goes deeper than 'how are you'.

conversation.speaker: A
conversation.text: What are you working on at the moment?

conversation.speaker: B
conversation.text: Mostly the migration. It's slower than we hoped.

conversation.speaker: A
conversation.text: What's holding it up?

conversation.speaker: B
conversation.text: Old data. Nobody documented any of it.

remember: Following up with 'what's holding it up?' turns polite small talk into a real conversation.

purpose: Start a conversation around a shared interest — food, places, films.

conversation.speaker: A
conversation.text: Have you tried the new place on the corner?

conversation.speaker: B
conversation.text: Not yet — is it any good?

conversation.speaker: A
conversation.text: Really good, but go early. It fills up.

conversation.speaker: B
conversation.text: Noted. What did you have?

keyExpressions: Not yet — is it any good?
remember: 'Is it any good?' is the natural everyday way to ask for an opinion about a place or product.

purpose: Ask someone's honest impression of a new job, city, or course.

conversation.speaker: A
conversation.text: You've been here a month now — how are you finding it?

conversation.speaker: B
conversation.text: Better than I expected, honestly. The team's been very welcoming.

conversation.speaker: A
conversation.text: Good. Anything you're still getting used to?

conversation.speaker: B
conversation.text: The commute. That I'm not enjoying.

keyExpressions: Anything you're still getting used to?
remember: This asks for a real opinion, unlike 'how are you'. Expect and give a genuine answer.

purpose: Open a conversation around news, sport, or something everyone is talking about.

conversation.speaker: A
conversation.text: Did you see the match last night?

conversation.speaker: B
conversation.text: Only the second half. What a finish.

conversation.speaker: A
conversation.text: I couldn't watch the last ten minutes.

remember: Choose a topic that is genuinely widely shared. A niche reference leaves the other person with nothing to say.

term: Sorry, I didn't catch your name
purpose: Recover politely when you have missed or forgotten someone's name.

conversation.speaker: A
conversation.text: Sorry, I didn't catch your name.

conversation.speaker: B
conversation.text: It's Nkechi.

conversation.speaker: A
conversation.text: Nkechi — sorry, could you say it once more? I want to get it right.

conversation.speaker: B
conversation.text: Nn-KEH-chi.

conversation.speaker: A
conversation.text: Nkechi. Got it.

keyExpressions: Sorry, I didn't catch your name.
Could you say it once more?
I want to get it right.
remember: Asking twice to pronounce a name correctly is a compliment, not a failure. Guessing silently is worse.

purpose: Ask to sit with someone or join a group.

conversation.speaker: A
conversation.text: Mind if I join you?

conversation.speaker: B
conversation.text: Not at all, please do.

conversation.speaker: A
conversation.text: Thanks. Is this seat usually free?

conversation.speaker: B
conversation.text: Always. Nobody comes to this end of the canteen.

remember: 'Do you mind?' is answered with 'no' to give permission. 'Not at all' avoids the confusion entirely.

purpose: Invite someone's opinion on something you are both experiencing.

conversation.speaker: A
conversation.text: What did you think of the presentation?

conversation.speaker: B
conversation.text: Interesting, but a bit long. You?

conversation.speaker: A
conversation.text: Same. The last section was the useful part.

remember: 'What do you think of' asks for an opinion; 'what do you think about' asks for a fuller view. Both are correct.

purpose: Open with a stranger in a neighbourhood or local setting.

conversation.speaker: A
conversation.text: Are you from around here?

conversation.speaker: B
conversation.text: I live two streets away. Why, are you lost?

conversation.speaker: A
conversation.text: Slightly. I'm looking for a decent bakery.

conversation.speaker: B
conversation.text: Then you want the one behind the church, not the one on the high street.

keyExpressions: I live just around the corner.
Do you know anywhere good for…?
remember: Asking for a local recommendation is one of the easiest ways to start a friendly exchange with a stranger.

purpose: Open sympathetically with someone who looks tired or busy.

conversation.speaker: A
conversation.text: Long day?

conversation.speaker: B
conversation.text: You have no idea. Started at six.

conversation.speaker: A
conversation.text: Ouch. Nearly done?

conversation.speaker: B
conversation.text: One more hour, then I'm going straight to bed.

remember: Two-word openers like this work because they invite a story without demanding one.

purpose: Continue a relationship with someone you already know reasonably well.

conversation.speaker: A
conversation.text: How's the family? Is your son still at university?

conversation.speaker: B
conversation.text: Final year now. He's applying for jobs, so we barely hear from him.

conversation.speaker: A
conversation.text: That's the stage where they go quiet. Give him my regards.

remember: Remembering one detail from last time — a name, a course, a trip — is what makes this feel personal rather than routine.

purpose: Ask a stranger for practical information, which often opens a longer exchange.

conversation.speaker: A
conversation.text: Sorry, do you know if this bus goes to the museum?

conversation.speaker: B
conversation.text: It does, but the 14 is faster.

conversation.speaker: A
conversation.text: Ah, thanks. Does it run often?

conversation.speaker: B
conversation.text: Every ten minutes or so.

remember: 'Do you know if…' is more polite than a direct question, because it lets the person say no without seeming unhelpful.

purpose: Greet someone returning from a holiday or long absence.

conversation.speaker: A
conversation.text: Welcome back! How was Japan?

conversation.speaker: B
conversation.text: Incredible. Exhausting, but incredible.

conversation.speaker: A
conversation.text: Where did you go in the end?

conversation.speaker: B
conversation.text: Tokyo, then Kyoto for a few days. I'd go back tomorrow.

keyExpressions: Where did you go in the end?
remember: Naming the place instead of asking 'how was your holiday' shows you remembered, and gets a warmer answer.
